title: Active and Passive Voice
tagline: Grammar · converting between voices without changing meaning

sourceNote.boardprep: All rules, tables, example sentences, questions and answers on this page are original BoardPrep material written for practice and are not taken from any textbook, guide or past paper.

overview.intro: Voice shows whether the subject of a sentence does the action or receives it. In the active voice the subject acts: The girl painted the wall. In the passive voice the subject receives the action: The wall was painted by the girl. Changing voice is a common exercise because it tests your knowledge of tenses, participles and pronouns together. The meaning and the tense must stay the same.

facts.label: Passive voice
facts.value: Object becomes subject + form of be + past participle (+ by the doer)

facts.label: Only for
facts.value: Transitive verbs, which take an object

facts.label: Golden rule
facts.value: The tense of the sentence must not change

facts.label: Watch
facts.value: Pronouns change form: I becomes me, he becomes him, they becomes them, and back

blocks.text: A passive sentence puts the receiver of the action first. It is useful when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious (The shop was robbed last night), or when the receiver matters more (The bridge was designed by a young engineer). Only verbs that take an object can be made passive. A sentence such as The baby slept has no object, so it has no passive form.

items.text: Active: The chef prepared the meal. Passive: The meal was prepared by the chef.
items.note: Object (the meal) becomes the subject; the verb becomes was prepared; the old subject follows by.

items.text: Active: Someone has stolen my bicycle. Passive: My bicycle has been stolen.
items.note: The doer is unknown, so by someone is left out.

items: Step 1. Find the subject, verb and object of the active sentence.
Step 2. Move the object to the front as the new subject. Change the pronoun if needed (me, him, her, us, them become I, he, she, we, they).
Step 3. Keep the tense. Use the matching form of be followed by the past participle of the main verb.
Step 4. Make the form of be agree with the new subject in number.
Step 5. Add by plus the old subject (changed to object form) if the doer is important. Leave it out if it is unknown, obvious or unimportant.
Step 6. Keep everything else, such as time and place phrases, in the sentence.

items.meaning: am, is or are + past participle. Active: She writes letters. Passive: Letters are written by her.
am, is or are being + past participle. The cook is preparing dinner. Dinner is being prepared by the cook.
has or have been + past participle. They have cancelled the match. The match has been cancelled.
was or were + past participle. He broke the window. The window was broken by him.
was or were being + past participle. They were repairing the road. The road was being repaired.
had been + past participle. The guard had locked the gate. The gate had been locked by the guard.
will or shall be + past participle. The committee will announce the results. The results will be announced by the committee.
will have been + past participle. She will have finished the report. The report will have been finished by her.
modal + be + past participle. You must submit the form. The form must be submitted.
Keep the question order. Did she write this poem? Was this poem written by her? Who wrote this letter? By whom was this letter written?
Use let + object + be + past participle. Post this letter. Let this letter be posted.

items.text: The gardener waters the plants every morning. Passive: The plants are watered by the gardener every morning.
The teacher is checking the notebooks. Passive: The notebooks are being checked by the teacher.
The boys have won the trophy. Passive: The trophy has been won by the boys.
items.note: The subject trophy is singular, so has been.

items.text: The teacher gave the students homework. Passive: The students were given homework by the teacher. Or: Homework was given to the students by the teacher.
items.note: Two objects give two possible passives. The first is more usual.

items.text: Nobody had seen the thief. Passive: The thief had not been seen by anyone.
items.note: A negative subject is changed to a negative verb plus anyone.

items.text: Who painted this picture? Passive: By whom was this picture painted?
items.note: A question with who becomes by whom.

items.text: Meera won the prize and the principal handed her the trophy. Passive: The prize was won by Meera and the trophy was handed to her by the principal.

learn.title: Common mistakes and how to correct them

items.text: Wrong: The cake was eaten by we. Right: The cake was eaten by us.
items.note: After by, use the object form of the pronoun.

items.text: Wrong: The letter was write by her. Right: The letter was written by her.
items.note: Use the past participle after be, not the base form.

items.text: Wrong: The window is broke. Right: The window is broken.
items.note: Broke is the past form; broken is the participle.

items.text: Wrong: The match is being played yesterday. Right: The match was played yesterday.
items.note: The tense must match the time.

items.text: Wrong: A poem was written by the girls. (from: The girls wrote the poems.) Right: The poems were written by the girls.
items.note: Keep the number of the object: poems is plural.

items.text: Wrong: The baby was slept by the mother. Right: The baby slept.

items: Step 1. Label the sentence: subject, verb, object. If there is no object, the sentence cannot be made passive.
Step 2. Name the tense of the verb before you change anything.
Step 3. Write the new subject, then the correct form of be for that tense and number, then the past participle.
Step 4. Decide whether to keep by plus the doer. Drop it when it is a vague word such as someone, people or they.
Step 5. Check pronouns and the time or place phrase.
Step 6. Read the new sentence and confirm the tense and meaning are unchanged.
When converting from passive to active, reverse the steps: the by phrase becomes the subject, and the tense of be tells you the tense of the active verb.

keyPoints: In the active voice the subject does the action; in the passive voice the subject receives it.
Only transitive verbs (verbs with an object) can be made passive.
The passive is formed with a form of be plus the past participle.
The tense of the sentence never changes when the voice changes.
Use present continuous passive is being and past continuous passive was being.
Drop by plus the doer when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant.
Questions keep their order; commands and requests use let.
Pronouns change form: after by use me, him, her, us, them.
examFocus: Changing active sentences into the passive and passive sentences into the active.
Handling different tenses and modal verbs correctly.
Using the past participle of irregular verbs correctly.
Recognising when the by phrase should be left out.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The chef is preparing the meal.
options: The meal is prepared by the chef.
The meal was being prepared by the chef.
The meal is being prepared by the chef.
The meal has been prepared by the chef.
questions.answer: The meal is being prepared by the chef.
questions.explanation: The active verb is in the present continuous, so the passive uses is being plus the past participle.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the simple present passive and losing the sense of an action in progress.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: They have cancelled the match.
questions.explanation: Present perfect active (have cancelled) becomes has been cancelled. The doer they is vague and is dropped.
questions.commonMistake: Changing the tense to the past perfect.

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences cannot be changed into the passive voice?
questions.explanation: Slept is intransitive and there is no object to become the subject of a passive sentence.
questions.commonMistake: Trying to force a passive from a verb without an object.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Who wrote this letter?
options: By whom this letter was written?
Who has been written this letter?
By whom was this letter written?
questions.answer: By whom was this letter written?
questions.explanation: A who question in the simple past becomes By whom was ... written? in the passive.
questions.commonMistake: Using statement word order in a question.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct passive form of the verb: The bridge ___ (build) in 1998.
questions.explanation: A definite past time and a singular subject give was plus the past participle.
questions.commonMistake: Writing was build or is built.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct passive form of the verb: The report must ___ (submit) before Friday.
questions.explanation: A modal verb is followed by be and the past participle in the passive.
questions.commonMistake: Leaving out be after the modal.

questions.prompt: Change into the passive voice: The gardener waters the plants every morning.
questions.answer: The plants are watered by the gardener every morning.
questions.explanation: Simple present: the object plants becomes the subject, the verb becomes are watered, and the doer follows by.
questions.commonMistake: Writing The plants is watered. The new subject is plural.

questions.prompt: Change into the passive voice: Nobody had seen the thief.
questions.answer: The thief had not been seen by anyone.
questions.explanation: Past perfect becomes had been seen. Nobody becomes not ... by anyone. The thief had been seen by nobody is less natural.
questions.commonMistake: Keeping nobody and adding not as well, which makes a double negative.

questions.prompt: Change into the passive voice: The teacher gave the students some homework.
questions.answer: The students were given some homework by the teacher.
questions.explanation: The verb gave has two objects, so two passives are possible. The other is: Some homework was given to the students by the teacher. The main answer above is more usual.
questions.commonMistake: Making the passive with the wrong number of the verb, such as was given for a plural subject.

questions.prompt: Change into the passive voice: Post this letter today.
questions.answer: Let this letter be posted today.
questions.explanation: Commands are turned into the passive with let, the object, be and the past participle. You are requested to post this letter today is not a passive form.
questions.commonMistake: Writing This letter is posted today, which is a statement, not a command.

questions.prompt: State two situations in which the passive voice is preferred to the active voice, with an example of each.
questions.answer: The passive is preferred when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious: My purse was stolen in the market. It is also useful when the receiver of the action is more important than the doer: The vaccine was developed by a small team of scientists.
questions.explanation: Two reasons with suitable examples earn full credit. Another valid reason is to keep the focus on the same subject across sentences.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the passive is more polite or more correct in general. It is simply a different focus.

questions.prompt: Change into the active voice: The prize was won by Meera, and the trophy was handed to her by the principal.
questions.answer: Meera won the prize, and the principal handed her the trophy.
questions.explanation: Each clause is converted separately. The by phrases become the subjects and the past tense is kept. The principal handed the trophy to her is also acceptable.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to change her to the correct form or leaving one clause in the passive.
